[Various dialectical forms: niyata (Sanskrit), niyata (Ardha-Magadhi), ṇiyaya (Ardha-Magadhi)]

(a) Certain through the Sotāpatti-magga (Stream-entry path) - Made certain through the Noble Path of Stream-entry. Certain for the sake of higher paths, having an unchangeable nature, certain to give results in the immediate future (sammatta-niyata-dhamma).
Root word analysis:
- niyata (adj.) [niyata + ṇa]: One who possesses either micchatta-niyata-dhamma (certainly wrong) or sammatta-niyata-dhamma (certainly right)
- niyata (adj.) [nij + ta]: Self-arising, self-dependent (fixed, firm, bound, compared, controlled kotthubha)
- niyata (adj.) [ni + ya + ta]: Unwavering, fixed, certain
- niyata (adj.) [niyata + ārammaṇa]: Having a fixed object
- niyata (m.) [ni + yamu + ta]: Decision, abstention

niyāma: [Ni+yamu+ṇa.(niyāma-saṃ]  CL=7 Firmness or Orderliness. (The Five Niyāma Dhammas): (1) Kamma niyāma – the law of kamma: wholesome kamma brings good results and unwholesome kamma brings bad results. (2) Utu-niyāma –the law of seasons: trees blossom and bear fruits according to the seasons. (3) Bīja-niyāma – the law of seeds: bitter seeds produce bitter fruits, sweet seeds produce sweet fruits — the nature of cause and effect in seeds. (4) Citta-niyāma – the law of mind: mental events arise in a fixed sequence, such as the arising of a resultant consciousness (sampaticchana citta) following eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa). (5) Dhamma-niyāma – the law of nature or phenomena: natural occurrences such as earthquakes happening at the birth of a Bodhisatta (future Buddha) — events that happen due to the inherent nature of reality.
